extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of early 18th-century periodicals; literary scholars; editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative remarks about producing, editing, and judging early-18th-century periodical essays (exemplified by The Tatler): aims, tone, organisation, textual-editing practice, and reception. Useful for editors, literary critics, and historians of the periodical press.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose: expose false arts and recommend simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The general purpose of this paper is to expose the false arts of life, to pull off the disguises of cunning, vanity, and affectation, and to recommend a general simplicity in our dress, our discourse, and our behaviour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The periodical should aim to correct vices and pretences in society and to promote simplicity and virtue; pieces should have a reforming moral intent rather than mere outrage or malicious gossip. Steele states satisfaction if the paper can 'destroy a single vice' or 'give a morning's cheerfulness to an honest mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction combined with entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: “to instruct the public what to think, after their reading, and there was to be something for the entertainment of the fair sex.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles should both shape readers' opinions (instruction) and provide entertainment—including material specifically aimed at female readers. Balance didactic aims with amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency, format and price
rubrics_metrics.description: “The numbers were published three times a week, on the post-days, at the price of one penny. Each paper consisted of a single folio sheet, and the first four were distributed gratuitously.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful periodical may use frequent, inexpensive issues to build readership; concise single-sheet issues and early free distribution can attract readers and coffee-house discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise content by topical headings (coffee-house rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The subject of each article was to be indicated by the name of the coffee-house or other place from which it was supposed to come: 'All accounts of gallantry, pleasure, and entertainment shall be under the article of White's Chocolate-house; Poetry, under that of Will's Coffee-house; Learning, under the title of Grecian; Foreign and Domestic News you will have from Saint James's Coffee-house; and what else I have to offer on any other subject shall be dated from my own Apartment.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent organisational scheme (here, fictive coffee-house headings) to signal topic and create familiar beats for readers. This clarifies expectations and lends colour/authority to items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with humour/raillery before severity
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was too soon to give my discourse on this subject so serious a turn; you have chiefly to do with that part of mankind which must be led into reflection by degrees, and you must treat this custom with humour and raillery to get an audience, before you come to pronounce sentence upon it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin reforming or critical essays with wit and mild ridicule to secure an audience; reserve stern judgment for later, once readers are engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genial satire and use of veiled/imaginary figures
rubrics_metrics.description: “Follies and weaknesses are ridiculed in the Tatler in a genial spirit... point is usually given to the papers by a sketch of some veiled or imaginary individual.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer genial, character-based satire (veiled or fictional individuals) rather than direct personal attacks. This preserves humour and moral force without alienating readers or provoking undue retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop sustained essays on morals and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: “the principal change... was the development of the sustained essay on morals or manners, and the less frequent indulgence in satire upon individual offenders, and in personal allusions in general.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over time, favor longer, reflective essays on general morals and manners rather than episodic gossip or lampooning specific persons—this gives work lasting value and broader appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar social scenes to illustrate lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: “its contributors made use of the scenes and events familiar to their readers in order to bring home the kindly lessons they wished to teach; and in so doing they have given us a picture of the daily life of the town which would alone have given lasting interest to the paper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground essays in everyday locations (coffee-houses, playhouses, exchanges, parks, shops) and common social events so moral points feel immediate and recognizable to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on domestic life, humane sympathy, and respect for women
rubrics_metrics.description: “It has been a most exquisite pleasure to me to frame characters of domestic life... there is nowhere better evidence than in the Tatler... his respect for women... he was the first of our writers who really seemed to admire and respect them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature domestic scenes and sympathetic portraits; cultivate empathy, tenderness, and respect for women—these traits increase moral authority and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate taste through informed literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Steele's teaching on morals and right living enters intimately into his literary criticism. His love for Shakespeare was real and intelligent... allusions to 'Paradise Lost'.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literary reference and criticism (canonical authors like Shakespeare and Milton) to encourage higher aesthetic standards and to illustrate moral or dramatic points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure actions, not parties; avoid partisan invective
rubrics_metrics.description: “The censure was to be of the actions of men, not of parties; and the design was to expose not persons but things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing public life, target conduct and social practices rather than political parties or factional attacks; this helps maintain moral credibility and broader readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame each number with a relevant quotation or motto
rubrics_metrics.description: “the motto of the first forty numbers was 'Quicquid agunt homines ... nostri farrago libelli'; but in the following numbers it was changed to 'Celebrare domestica facta'; and afterwards each number generally had a quotation bearing upon the subject of the day.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a motto or topical quotation to frame and focus each issue or essay; it signals theme and lends literary authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurring dramatis personae as a flexible framework
rubrics_metrics.description: “Isaac Bickerstaff himself... is rather vaguely sketched, and his familiar, Pacolet... The occasional references to Bickerstaff's half-sister, Jenny Distaff... gave Steele a framework for some charming sketches of domestic life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring fictional or persona elements (e.g., a pseudonymous editor, club members) can provide continuity and a narrative device, but need not dominate content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual-editing standard: aim for scrupulous accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Scrupulous accuracy in the text has been aimed at, but the eccentricities of spelling--which were the printer's, not the author's--have not been preserved, and the punctuation has occasionally been corrected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should pursue close textual accuracy, correct printer's eccentricities, and standardize punctuation cautiously; preserve authorial intent while removing clear transmission errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve valuable annotations from older editions; supplement concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have endeavoured to preserve what is of value in the older editions, and to supplement it, as concisely as possible, by such further information as appeared desirable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing annotated editions, retain useful historical notes from earlier editors and add concise, targeted supplemental information rather than excessive footnoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary primary sources to clarify obscure passages
rubrics_metrics.description: “The eighteenth-century diaries and letters published of late years have in many cases enabled me to throw light on passages which have hitherto been obscure, and sometimes useful illustrations have been found in the contemporary newspapers and periodicals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ diaries, letters, and contemporary newspapers to illuminate historical references, people, and events; such research can materially improve annotation and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate edition with authentic contemporary engravings
rubrics_metrics.description: “The portraits of Steele, Addison, and Swift, the writers most associated with the Tatler, have been taken from contemporary engravings in the British Museum; and the imaginary portrait of Isaac Bickerstaff in the last volume is from a rare picture drawn by Lens in 1710.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include portraits and illustrations sourced from contemporary engravings or authentic images to enhance historical authenticity and reader engagement; where none exist, careful imagined portraiture may be used with clear acknowledgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing tactic: give away initial issues to build readership
rubrics_metrics.description: “the first four were distributed gratuitously.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider gratis distribution of inaugural issues to seed readership and stimulate discussion in social venues (coffee-houses, clubs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance gossip/social reportage with instructive moral content
rubrics_metrics.description: “Though it is not true... that the Tatler is for the most part a mere society journal... the social articles are at least as interesting now as when they were written... combining wisdom with satire.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine lively social reportage and gossip with instructive essays—do not simply pander to fashionable vices; use social material as vehicle for moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive personal allusions and individual lampooning as series matures
rubrics_metrics.description: “the less frequent indulgence in satire upon individual offenders, and in personal allusions in general.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a periodical becomes established, reduce direct lampooning of named individuals and rely more on general sketches and types to preserve longevity and respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and personification where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference in text to 'the allegorical paper on Fælicia, or Britain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ allegory and personification to treat national or abstract subjects imaginatively; such devices can broaden appeal and moral reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of political and personal risk when attacking swindlers or parties
rubrics_metrics.description: “The campaign against swindlers exposed Steele to serious threats on more than one occasion... events of 1710, which led to the discontinuance of the Tatler... Steele lost his post of Gazetteer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors should weigh the risks of direct attacks on powerful figures, institutions, or swindlers; political engagement can threaten positions and continuity of publication.
